title: Instruction Formats & Encoding
summary: How opcode, register, and immediate fields pack into an instruction word, and the trade-off between fixed and variable-length encoding.

slides.markdown:
Every instruction word is a bit pattern split into **fields** the decoder knows how to read: an **opcode** (which operation), one or more **register operands** (which registers), and sometimes an **immediate/offset** (a constant baked into the instruction itself).

The opcode is always first — the decoder needs to know *what* the instruction is before it can make sense of the rest of the bits. Everything after that is opcode-specific: an `add` reads two register fields; a `load` reads a register plus an offset.

This fixed layout is what lets hardware decode millions of instructions per second without ambiguity.

slides.subTitle: Worked bit layout
slides.markdown:
A 32-bit R-type word (register-to-register operation) in a MIPS/RISC-V-style ISA, bit-field by bit-field:

![Bit layout of a 32-bit R-type instruction word: opcode, source registers, destination register, function code](assets/rtype-encoding.svg)

The **opcode** narrows the instruction family; the **funct** field (when present) selects the exact operation within that family — this is how a small opcode space still supports dozens of distinct instructions.

assets.alt: Bit layout of a 32-bit R-type instruction word: opcode, source registers, destination register, function code

slides.markdown:
**Fixed-length encoding** gives every instruction the exact same width (e.g., 32 bits for classic RISC-V/MIPS/ARM). The decoder always knows exactly where each field starts — no scanning required.

The cost: bits are spent on every instruction whether it needs them or not, so **immediates are cramped** (a 32-bit instruction can't embed a full 32-bit constant and still leave room for an opcode and registers) and simple instructions waste width they don't use.

Fixed-length is what makes RISC's simple, predictable pipelining possible.

**Variable-length encoding** (x86's hallmark) lets each instruction be exactly as wide as it needs — 1 byte for a trivial operation, 15 for a complex one with a large immediate and prefixes.

The payoff is **code density**: real programs are smaller in memory and use less instruction-cache space. The cost is a genuinely harder decode stage — the CPU must partially parse an instruction just to learn how long it is, which complicates fetching multiple instructions per cycle.

This is a major reason x86 decoders are more complex than RISC decoders.

The trade-off in one table:

| | Fixed-length | Variable-length |
|---|---|---|
| Decode complexity | Low — field positions known | High — must parse to find length |
| Code density | Lower — wasted bits | Higher — compact common ops |
| Multi-issue fetch | Easy — jump N bytes per instruction | Hard — must decode to find next boundary |
| Typical family | RISC (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS) | CISC (x86) |

Decide by asking: does the ISA prioritize a **simple, fast decode pipeline** or **maximal code density**? RISC bets on the former; CISC historically bet on the latter, when memory was the scarce resource.

Given a 32-bit R-type word `0x00A63020` in a MIPS-style format (opcode 6 bits, rs 5, rt 5, rd 5, shamt 5, funct 6):

```
binary:  000000 00101 00110 00110 00000 100000
fields:  opcode  rs     rt    rd   shamt funct
         000000  $5    $6    $6    0     100000
```

```
opcode = 0      -> R-type instruction
rs     = 5      -> register $5
rt     = 6      -> register $6
rd     = 6      -> register $6 (destination)
funct  = 0x20   -> ADD
```

So the word decodes to `add $6, $5, $6` — this is exactly what a disassembler automates.

slides.subTitle: Immediates that don't fit
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Any constant can just go directly into one instruction."

**Why it's wrong:** a fixed-length 32-bit instruction only has so many bits left over after the opcode and register fields — often just 12–16 bits for an immediate. A large 32-bit constant simply doesn't fit.

**Correct model:** ISAs handle this by building the constant across **multiple instructions** — e.g., RISC-V's `lui` (load upper immediate) followed by `addi` for the lower bits. This is a direct, visible consequence of fixed-length encoding's cramped immediate fields, not a compiler bug.

slides.sectionTitle: Branch offsets have a limited range
slides.subTitle: What happens when a jump is too far
slides.markdown:
A PC-relative branch's offset lives in the same cramped immediate field as everything else — RISC-V's conditional branches encode only a 12-bit signed offset (roughly +-4KB), and even its `jal` unconditional jump caps out around +-1MB. A branch target further away than the field can express **cannot be encoded directly**.

When the assembler or linker discovers a branch target is out of range, it must synthesize a longer sequence — load the full target address into a register (across multiple instructions, as in the previous pitfall) and jump through the register instead of using the compact direct-offset form. This is invisible in source code but shows up as extra instructions purely because two pieces of code ended up far apart in the final binary layout.

slides.subTitle: Compressed instruction extensions
slides.markdown:
RISC-V's **C (compressed) extension** and ARM's **Thumb** mode take a middle path between pure fixed-length and pure variable-length: common instructions (moving a register, a small immediate add, a frequent branch) get a compact 16-bit encoding, while the full 32-bit encoding remains available for everything else — and the two are freely mixed in the same instruction stream, distinguished by a marker in the first bits.

This captures most of variable-length's code-density win (real programs are dominated by a small set of frequent, simple instructions that compress well) while keeping the *decode* problem far simpler than x86's fully general variable length, since there are only two possible widths to check for, not an open-ended range.
